claims.text: The identity of X (Si, Mn, or Al) governs protective-oxide formation and persistence in CrFeCoNiX above 900 °C.
X controls oxidation behavior by modulating oxygen diffusivity at the oxide–metal boundary.
X controls oxidation behavior by modulating interfacial stress relaxation.
Al additions preferentially form a thermodynamically stable, slowly growing, coherent, and adherent Al2O3 scale.
Si additions preferentially form a thermodynamically stable, slowly growing, coherent, and adherent SiO2 scale.
Mn additions form oxides with relatively high oxygen diffusivity.
Mn-related oxides have unfavorable mechanical properties that promote cracking and spallation.
The proposed comparison uses a CrFeCoNi baseline and variants containing 5–10 at.% Si, Mn, or Al.
The X additions are to be uniformly alloyed, with processing and alloy homogeneity controlled.
Al and Si reduce oxygen solubility and diffusivity in the CrFeCoNiX substrate.
Al and Si facilitate stress relaxation at the oxide–metal interface.
Mn oxides cannot effectively impede oxygen penetration or accommodate interfacial stresses.
Al- and Si-containing alloys will exhibit slow parabolic oxidation kinetics and retain continuous, adherent scales.
Mn-containing alloys will oxidize faster, may show linear kinetics, and will develop porous or cracked scales that spall.
The CrFeCoNi baseline is expected to have intermediate oxidation behavior without the enhanced stability attributed to Al or Si.
The hypothesis applies to single- or multiphase solid-solution CrFeCoNiX alloys above 900 °C in oxidative or corrosive environments.
A controlled test will expose identically processed alloys at 950 °C for 10, 50, and 100 hours and compare scale morphology, thickness, adhesion, phases, mass gain, and interfacial stress.
Comparable or inferior scale protection from Al- or Si-containing alloys relative to the baseline or Mn variants, or a similarly protective Mn scale, would falsify the hypothesis.
